newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Aer Lingus '96 pretax profit soars 130 pct.
newsitem.headline: Aer Lingus '96 pretax profit soars 130 pct.

text.p: Ireland's Aer Lingus said on Wednesday that pre-tax profits soared by 130 percent to 40.9 million Irish pounds last year but warned that continued cost reductions were essential for future profitability.
The national airline said two non-trading factors contributed significantly to the sharp improvement in profit at pre-tax level.

The net interest charge fell to 1.3 million in 1996 from 20.4 million a year earlier while exceptional items contributed 4.4 million against 1995's charge of 11.7 million as the airline wrote back prior year provisions no longer required.
Aer Lingus said in a statement that it recorded strong growth on all major route groups, a solid performance from its cargo division and an improving result for subsidiary companies.

Operating profit from continuing businesses, a key measure of the trading performance of the group, rose by four percent to 41.8 million Irish pounds while turnover was up nine percent at 766 million.
The airline said transatlantic traffic grew strongly, reflecting its new services to Chicago while the New York and Boston routes performed well.

UK traffic growth was also good, especially in business class, while continental European traffic was strong, supported by additional services and the extension of the airline's Premier service to all mainland European destinations.
Aer Lingus said its cargo division also turned in a good performance with U.S. Midwest market consolidation assisted by the new Chicago passenger service.
Overall, the air transport division reported an operating profit of 42.2 million, down from 43.6 million in 1995.
Other operations contributed a trading loss of 0.4 million, compared to a loss of 3.4 million a year earlier.
The group's aircraft maintenance subsidiary, TEAM Aer Lingus, achieved a strong second-half performance and extended its market presence in tough trading conditions.
It aimed to break even by 1999, Aer Lingus said.
Chairman Bernie Cahill said the group made significant further progress last year but warned that the 1996 results were achieved during a period of considerable buoyancy.
It was widely accepted by sector analysts that the industry was probably at the top of its trade cycle, he said.
"It is clear that sustained effort is vital if we are to achieve the further cost reductions in unit costs which are an essential prerequisite to profitability," Cahill said.
Aer Lingus said an important aspect of performance was the continued strengthening of the balance sheet as result of strong cashflow from operations and the sale of non-core assets.

The group had a net cash balance of 38.7 million Irish pounds at end-December 1996 compared to net debt of 41.4 million a year earlier while shareholders' funds grew by 21 percent to 190.5 million in 1996.

Aer Lingus chief executive Gary McGann said rebuilding the balance sheet was vital given the airline's sensitivity to even apparently small percentage changes in many cost areas because of the low margin sectors in which it operated.

"As our business becomes increasingly competitive, it will be difficult to grow those margins. It is vital, therefore, that Aer Lingus should maintain its strong emphasis on the task of rebuilding its balance sheet while expanding its core business."
